scope: Evaluates the owner's 40 candidates plus 8 discovered while reading the code. Analysis is grounded in the code as it stands on 2026-07-24, not in a generic product.

productSnapshot.note: Every figure below was counted from the files named. Nothing here is estimated.

bridgeOperations.designNote: An allowlist. There is no generic exec verb, so every candidate that needs a new capability is a protocol change, not a UI change. This is the single largest cost driver in the matrix.

prototypeStatuses.gap: The UI layer models 7 states; the bridge contract models 23. Nine of the 23 (WAITING_FOR_PERMISSION, STOPPING, INTERRUPTED, DISCONNECTED, RECOVERING, RESUMABLE, ORPHANED, FAILED_RECOVERY, DEGRADED) have no visual representation anywhere in the 13 views.

usageFields.gap: src/bridge/usage/aggregator.ts is 80 KB and no view renders a single one of these fields.

documentedShortcuts.contradiction: The reference table says Ctrl+Enter sends a message and the 'Send with' default is 'ctrl-enter'; src/views/chat/Composer.tsx sends on plain Enter.

searchSurfaces.detail: Sidebar (store projectQuery), Home (same store field), Files (local useState), Activity (local useState), Command palette (fuzzy over commands + project names). None of them reads a message body, a proof reason, an artifact preview or a file's contents.

networkPosture.consequence: A headless always-on box is reachable only by screen sharing into it. Any candidate whose value depends on reaching the workspace from a second device is out of scope until the owner changes that posture.

productSnapshot.knownDebt: src/components/primitives/Icon.tsx resolves lucide icons by runtime name, defeating tree-shaking: 1.23 MB JS / 343 KB gzip (README.md, Known limitations).

decisionLegend.IMPLEMENT_NOW: Build it in the next block of work. Justified against the cost of not building it.
decisionLegend.IMPLEMENT_AS_OPT_IN: Build it, default off, behind an explicit switch. Reserved for things that interrupt or ask for a browser permission.
decisionLegend.DESIGN_FOR_LATER: Real value, but a stated precondition is not true yet. Each entry names the trigger that would reopen it.
decisionLegend.REJECT: Do not build. Either it duplicates something shipped, it contradicts a rule the product is built on, or it adds surface without adding capability.
decisionLegend.OWNER_APPROVAL_REQUIRED: Cannot be decided by an engineer. It changes what the workspace is permitted to do to the owner's machine or files.

counts.note: 41 entries cover the owner's 40 candidates (export is split into export-evidence-bundle and export-conversation, because the two have different redaction problems). 6 entries were discovered while reading the code: approval-queue, run-control, workspace-preference-persistence, composer-command-completion, event-gap-surface, static-icon-map.

features.name: Universal search
features.userProblem: There are five separate search fields (sidebar, Home, Files, Activity, command palette) and none of them can find the thing you actually go looking for: the sentence in a conversation where a decision was made, the proof entry that rejected a claim, or the event that preceded a failure. Finding anything today means remembering which of the 13 views it lives in first.
features.proposedBehaviour: One index, one entry point. Ctrl+K keeps opening the existing palette; typing a plain term (no leading '>' or ':') searches projects, conversation titles and message bodies, task titles and details, artifact names and previews, proof claims and reasons, event messages and details, and file paths. Results group by kind with the source view named on each row, and Enter navigates to the row's home view with the record already selected. The index is built in memory from what the bridge already returned; nothing extra is read from disk to service a keystroke.
features.securityImpact: Low, with one real trap: the index must be built from records the bridge already handed over, never by widening a read. It must also respect AttachmentRecord.claudeAccessible and never index a QUARANTINED or REJECTED attachment's contents.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent. The whole corpus is local and small; a linear scan with the existing fuzzyScore() in CommandPalette.tsx is fast enough for one owner's workspace without any index format on disk.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good. Keep the index in memory and rebuild it lazily on first search rather than eagerly on boot, so an always-on box is not holding a full-text index of every project it has ever opened.
features.testPlan: Unit (vitest): fuzzy ranking is stable and deterministic for a fixed corpus; a quarantined attachment never appears in results; each result kind resolves to a route + selection pair. E2E (playwright): from /activity, Ctrl+K, type a phrase that exists only in one message body, press Enter, assert the URL is /chat and the message is scrolled into view and focused.
features.rationale: Not building it means the workspace keeps growing surfaces that each own a fifth of the answer, which is the exact failure mode the owner asked to avoid.

features.name: Session health
features.userProblem: The topbar chip is a hard-coded string ('Claude Code · Local session · Not connected in prototype') that is not derived from anything — see the comment on ClaudeCodeChip in Topbar.tsx: 'Never derived from anything.' Once runs are real, a quiet window and a dead session look identical, and the nine loss-and-recovery statuses in the contract have nowhere to appear.
features.proposedBehaviour: The chip becomes the one honest read of ClaudeCodeStatus + BridgeHealth: CLI availability, resolved executable path, version, authenticated yes/no, uptime, active runs, last event time, and the degraded[] list verbatim. Its popover shows the current session id or the sentence 'no session reported' — never a placeholder. It renders RESUMABLE, ORPHANED, RECOVERING, FAILED_RECOVERY and DISCONNECTED as first-class states with icon + uppercase label + the status border treatment, and offers exactly one action per state (resumeSession where the state permits it, nothing where it does not).
features.securityImpact: Low but not zero: executablePath and projectsRoot are absolute paths on the owner's machine. They belong in the popover, not in a toast or an exported bundle that might be shared.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent. Every field already exists in BridgeHealth and ClaudeCodeStatus; this is presentation of data the bridge computes anyway.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent, and disproportionately valuable there: an always-on box is exactly where a session dies silently overnight. Drive it from bridge.heartbeat rather than a UI poll so the fanless box is not woken by the browser.
features.testPlan: Unit: a fixture per state renders the correct icon + UPPERCASE label + border token and offers only the actions that state permits; authenticated=false never renders as available. E2E: with the bridge stopped, the chip reads DISCONNECTED within the heartbeat window and no view claims a live session.
features.rationale: A workspace whose central claim is that a status is a claim about reality cannot ship a status chip that is a string literal.

features.name: Approval queue
features.userProblem: DISCOVERED. listApprovals / approveAction / denyAction, the ApprovalRequest record (risk, affects[], rollbackPlan, expiresAt), the WAITING_FOR_PERMISSION status and the approval.requested / approval.resolved events all exist in the contract — and no view in the product renders any of them. A run that pauses for permission today looks to the user like a run that hung.
features.proposedBehaviour: A seventh Dock panel, Approvals, plus a count badge on the dock rail and a topbar indicator when anything is pending. Each row shows the requesting agent, the action, the affected paths, the risk level as icon + UPPERCASE label, the rollback plan and the expiry as a live countdown. Approve and Deny are the only two buttons; both require the row to be expanded first so the rollback plan has been on screen before a decision is possible. An expired request is shown as EXPIRED and cannot be actioned.
features.securityImpact: This is the highest-consequence surface in the product — it is where a browser click widens what the CLI may do. Deny must be the default outcome of expiry, approval must be scoped to the single requestId, and an approval must never be inferable from a keyboard shortcut or a palette command.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent. Entirely local; the request and the decision never leave the machine.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good, with a caveat: on a headless box nobody sees a pending approval until they screen-share in. Pair it with background-notifications or accept that long runs stall until someone looks.
features.testPlan: Unit: an expired ApprovalRequest cannot be approved; approveAction is called with exactly one id; the rollback plan must have been rendered before the buttons enable. E2E: emit approval.requested, assert the dock badge appears, expand, approve, assert approval.resolved arrives and the badge clears.
features.rationale: Without it the only blocking interaction the product has is invisible, which turns every permission request into an apparent hang.

features.name: Run control — stop, cancel, resume
features.userProblem: DISCOVERED. stopRun, run.cancel.requested, run.cancelled, resumeSession and the STOPPING / CANCELLED / INTERRUPTED / RESUMABLE statuses all exist. The only Stop button in the entire UI is in the chat composer and it stops a setTimeout that reveals canned text (Composer.tsx / ChatView handleStop). When runs are real, Stop is the control the owner will reach for first and it has no reliable home.
features.proposedBehaviour: Stop is available wherever a run is visible — the composer, the Home 'Active mission' card, Mission Control's toolbar, the Activity run header. It is a two-state control: pressing it shows STOPPING (the request was sent) and only becomes CANCELLED when run.cancelled arrives, so the button never claims a kill it cannot prove. A run that ended as INTERRUPTED or RESUMABLE offers Resume in the same place, and a run that is ORPHANED offers nothing but an explanation.
features.securityImpact: Low. Stop only narrows what is happening. The care needed is honesty, not permission: never render CANCELLED before the bridge confirms it.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — it is a local process signal.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent. On an always-on box a runaway run burns quota and heat until someone stops it; this is the brake.
features.testPlan: Unit: the button transitions RUNNING → STOPPING on click and only reaches CANCELLED on run.cancelled; a second click while STOPPING is a no-op, not a second stopRun. E2E: start a run, stop it from Mission Control, assert the Activity feed shows run.cancel.requested followed by run.cancelled and the composer re-enables.
features.rationale: Every other feature here is about seeing; this is the only one about being able to intervene, and it is currently wired to a text-reveal timer.

features.name: Usage — as a bar, not a dashboard
features.userProblem: UsageSnapshot carries 20 provenance-labelled fields and src/bridge/usage/aggregator.ts is 80 KB. Not one of those numbers reaches a screen. The owner cannot see which model answered, how full the context window is, or whether a figure was reported by the CLI or estimated locally.
features.proposedBehaviour: Reject the 'dashboard' framing. Build one persistent strip under the composer and in the topbar showing: model, context percent as a thin meter, turns, tool calls, elapsed, and cost — each rendering its Accuracy so an ESTIMATED figure is visibly not an EXACT one, and an UNAVAILABLE field prints the honest absence rather than a zero. planUsage always prints PLAN_USAGE_UNAVAILABLE_MESSAGE. When stale is true the strip says so instead of showing an ageing number. getUsageHistory feeds a single sparkline of context growth across the conversation and nothing else.
features.securityImpact: None directly. The discipline is that a DERIVED total must only be arithmetic over EXACT values, as the protocol comment requires — a derived total that silently includes an estimate would launder an approximation into a fact.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent. All aggregation already happens in the bridge.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good. Cap the history the strip holds in memory; do not keep every snapshot of a month-long uptime.
features.testPlan: Unit: each Accuracy renders a distinct non-colour treatment; UNAVAILABLE never renders a numeral; a DERIVED total built over any ESTIMATED input is refused. E2E: with telemetry stopped, the strip shows the stale sentence within the staleness window.
features.rationale: This is the only surface where the product's provenance rules become visible to a user; a full analytics page would be a fourteenth view nobody opens twice.

features.name: Project templates
features.userProblem: HomeView already renders six template cards (TEMPLATES in HomeView.tsx) and every one of them fires a toast that says nothing was created. createProject exists in the contract, ProjectRecord carries templateVersion, and src/bridge/projects/create.ts is 62 KB. The UI and the bridge are both built and the wire between them is missing.
features.proposedBehaviour: The six cards open one small modal: name, parent folder (validated through the existing path guard), template, and a preview of exactly what will be written to disk. Confirm calls createProject and the resulting project.created event drives navigation. The written templateVersion is shown on the project overview so a project made in July is distinguishable from one made later.
features.securityImpact: Real — this is the browser causing directories and files to be written. Every path must go through the existing canonicalisation and trusted-root check; OUTSIDE_TRUSTED_ROOT and PATH_REJECTED must be surfaced as refusals, never swallowed.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — writing a project scaffold to a local folder is the definition of local-first.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent, if the parent folder is chosen explicitly each time rather than defaulting to a root the owner has forgotten about.
features.testPlan: Unit: reuse src/bridge/security/paths.test-vectors.ts against every path the modal can produce; a traversal attempt is refused with PATH_REJECTED and no directory is created. E2E: create a website project, assert it appears in the sidebar with the right type icon and that its overview shows the recorded templateVersion.
features.rationale: Six inert cards on the landing screen are the most visible unkept promise in the product, and both halves of the work already exist.

features.name: Project import
features.userProblem: importProject exists and src/bridge/projects/discover.ts is 25 KB, but nothing in the UI can point the workspace at an existing folder. Until that works, the only projects the workspace can hold are ones it created itself — which means it cannot be used on any work that already exists.
features.proposedBehaviour: One 'Import a folder' action next to 'New project' in the sidebar and on the projects screen. It runs discovery first and shows what was found before anything is recorded: git state (branch, dirty count, remote), whether a .claude/ install is present, detected project type, and the file count. Import records a ProjectRecord and nothing else — it never writes into the folder it is importing.
features.securityImpact: Read-only by contract, and it must stay that way. Discovery must not follow symlinks out of the chosen folder and must not read file contents — only structure and git metadata.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good with a guard: discovery over a folder containing node_modules or a large monorepo must be bounded by depth and entry count, or a fanless box will spin on it.
features.testPlan: Unit: discovery is bounded by depth and count; symlinks that escape the chosen root are ignored; a folder with no git returns initialized=false rather than a fabricated branch. E2E: import this repository and assert the overview shows the real branch and dirty-file count.
features.rationale: Without import the workspace can only manage work it invented, which makes every other feature here a demo.

features.name: Keyboard-first workflows
features.userProblem: SettingsView documents 20 shortcuts across four groups. The shell implements four of them globally (Ctrl+K, Ctrl+B, '/', Escape) and one documented shortcut actively contradicts the shipped behaviour: the table says Ctrl+Enter sends a message, the 'Send with' default is 'ctrl-enter', and Composer.tsx sends on plain Enter. A reference table that is mostly aspiration is the same category of dishonesty the rest of this codebase refuses.
features.proposedBehaviour: Close the gap in both directions. Implement Ctrl+I (inspector), Ctrl+J (dock), Ctrl+, (settings) and the G-prefixed navigation chords in AppShell alongside the existing handlers. Fix the composer contradiction by making 'Send with' a real preference that Composer reads. Delete any row from the table that will not be implemented, and derive the table from the same map the shell registers so the two can never drift again.
features.securityImpact: One rule: no shortcut may ever resolve to approveAction, denyAction or any write. Keyboard speed and irreversible actions do not belong on the same key.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good. Register the chords with metaKey as well as ctrlKey; the existing handlers already check both.
features.testPlan: Unit: a single exported shortcut map is the source of both the registrations and the settings table, and a test asserts every documented row has a registration. E2E: press each documented chord and assert the described effect; assert no chord triggers an approval.
features.rationale: The cheap alternative — deleting the sixteen unimplemented rows — is also acceptable, but the shortcuts are genuinely how this shell is meant to be driven, and shipping a table that lies about the product is not.

features.name: Export — proof and manifest bundle
features.userProblem: The product's thesis is that a claim carries evidence that can be re-checked later (EvidenceRef with a path and a hash, testPassed() derived from exit code and counts, a proof ledger where an unevidenced claim is rejected). None of that can leave the window. The evidence is only checkable by the person sitting at the machine, in the tab, at the time.
features.proposedBehaviour: One action on the Tests & proof screen: 'Export evidence bundle'. It writes a folder containing proof.jsonl (every ProofEntry in scope), tests.jsonl (every TestExecution with its exit code, counts and stdout/stderr refs), a manifest.json listing every EvidenceRef with its path and hash, and a README stating what the bundle does and does not prove. The bundle records gaps explicitly — a missing artifact is listed as missing, not omitted. artifacts/baseline-manifest.json is the existing precedent for the shape.
features.securityImpact: Highest of the IMPLEMENT_NOW set. A bundle is the one artefact designed to be shared, so it must never carry absolute machine paths, executablePath, projectsRoot, environment values, or attachment contents. It should reuse the redaction discipline already in src/bridge/attachments/policy.ts. Bundles are written to a folder the owner picks, never auto-uploaded — there is nowhere to upload to.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — a folder on disk is the natural output of a local-first evidence system.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good. Bound the bundle by run or by project, never 'everything', so a year of uptime is not one export.
features.testPlan: Unit: a bundle built over a fixture contains every EvidenceRef and marks missing artifacts as missing; a scan over the produced bundle finds no absolute path outside the project and no value matching the secret patterns in policy.ts. E2E: export from /tests and assert the manifest hash of a known artifact matches the file on disk.
features.rationale: Evidence that cannot leave the tab is evidence only the author can check, which is most of the way back to taking the claim on trust.

features.name: Workspace preference persistence
features.userProblem: DISCOVERED. Exactly two keys are persisted (appearance, density). Pins, the active project, the active conversation, sidebar/inspector/dock state, the dock tab, agent and task layouts, and every filter live in memory and are gone on reload. On a workspace you return to several times a day, re-establishing your view is the most frequently repeated action in the product.
features.proposedBehaviour: One versioned preferences record under .forge-workspace/ (the folder and its migrations.json already exist) holding: pinned project ids, last active project and conversation, shell region state, dock tab, per-view layout choices, and the last filter set per view. It restores on boot and is written debounced. It is preferences only — never a cache of records, so a stale preference can never make the workspace render data it did not just receive.
features.securityImpact: Low, and it improves one thing: the Data and privacy section currently lists two localStorage keys as the complete truth. That table must be updated in the same change, or the privacy screen becomes wrong the moment this ships.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent. Writing preferences to the workspace folder rather than to browser storage also means they survive a cleared cache.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent. Use the existing atomic write path so a preference write during a power cut cannot leave a truncated file.
features.testPlan: Unit: a preferences record from an older schemaVersion is migrated or discarded, never partially applied; a corrupt file falls back to defaults without throwing. E2E: pin a project, switch dock tab, reload, assert both survived and that no record data was restored from the preferences file.
features.rationale: It is the smallest change on this list and it removes friction that is paid every single time the window is opened.

features.name: Automatic conversation titles
features.userProblem: ConversationRecord.title has to come from somewhere. Left to a human it becomes 'Untitled conversation' forty times over, and the sidebar's recent-conversations list — which is the main way back into work — becomes useless.
features.proposedBehaviour: Derive the title deterministically from the first user message: first sentence, collapsed whitespace, capped at ~60 characters, with a trailing ellipsis when truncated. No model call. The title is editable and an edited title is never overwritten. If the first message is empty or is only an attachment, the title is the attachment's filename.
features.securityImpact: One consideration: a title is shown in the sidebar and could be in an export, so the first line of a message becomes more visible than the rest. That is acceptable for the owner's own machine, and it is a reason to keep titles out of the evidence bundle.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — string handling, no runtime involvement.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent.
features.testPlan: Unit: fixed inputs produce fixed titles (deterministic, no clock or random); an edited title survives a further message; a message of only whitespace falls back rather than producing an empty title.
features.rationale: The model-generated variant would spend the owner's own plan quota on every new thread while planUsage is UNAVAILABLE and cannot show what it cost — a deterministic first-sentence title is a fraction of the work and none of the cost.

features.name: Local audit log
features.userProblem: The bridge already writes one (writeAudit / AuditEntry in src/bridge/router.ts: timestamp, bridge instance, requestId, op, projectId, clientId, transport, outcome, error code, duration) and it already emits bridge.degraded when a line cannot be written. Nothing in the UI shows it. The strongest security claim the product makes — that the browser can only ask for 39 named things and every ask is recorded — is currently unverifiable from inside the product.
features.proposedBehaviour: A read-only Audit view reachable from Settings → Data and privacy: the ledger newest-first with filters for operation, outcome and error code, a visible count of REJECTED and ERROR outcomes, and a plain statement when the ledger is incomplete because a write failed. Read-only by construction — there is no delete and no edit, and that is stated on the screen.
features.securityImpact: Positive on balance, with one rule: the ledger already passes values through ledgerSafe() and must keep doing so. The view must never render a payload — only the envelope. A payload in an audit line is how a secret ends up in a log.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — the ledger is a local append-only file and never leaves the machine.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good, with rotation: an always-on box accumulates ledger lines indefinitely. Read the tail by default and make 'load more' explicit.
features.testPlan: Unit: the view renders no field outside the AuditEntry shape; a degraded ledger renders the incompleteness notice rather than a clean list. E2E: issue an unknown operation, assert a REJECTED line with UNKNOWN_OPERATION appears in the audit view.
features.rationale: The ledger is already written; leaving it invisible means the product asks to be trusted on exactly the point it has already built the receipt for.

features.name: In-app notifications
features.userProblem: Toasts exist and are capped at four, and the Dock has a Notices panel of standing facts. Neither survives a view change, and there is no route from a background event to your attention. SettingsView already draws five notification switches that do nothing.
features.proposedBehaviour: Make the existing switches real for three events only — approval.requested, verify.verdict = REJECTED, and run finished (completed or failed). Delivery is a count on the document title and a badge on the dock rail; the toast escalates only for approvals. Quiet hours suppresses the title count. No notification centre, no history list, no per-event configuration beyond those three switches.
features.securityImpact: Notification text must not carry paths or command lines — 'a run needs permission' rather than the action itself, with the detail behind a click.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good, but limited — a title-bar count is useless on a screen nobody is looking at. See background-notifications.
features.testPlan: Unit: each switch gates exactly its own event and nothing else; quiet hours suppresses delivery without suppressing the underlying event. E2E: with the tab backgrounded, emit approval.requested and assert the document title carries the count.
features.rationale: Anything that interrupts should be chosen rather than inherited, and three events is the whole set that has ever justified an interruption in this product.

features.name: Background (OS) notifications
features.userProblem: A long run on an always-on box finishes, or stops for permission, while nobody is looking at the window. Without an OS-level signal the only way to know is to keep checking, which is exactly the babysitting the multi-agent design exists to remove.
features.proposedBehaviour: Off by default. A single switch in Settings → Notifications requests the browser Notification permission at the moment it is turned on, and never before. It fires for the same three events as in-app notifications, at most one per event, with no body text beyond the event kind and the project name. If permission is denied, the switch reverts and says so plainly rather than staying on and silently doing nothing.
features.securityImpact: This is the only browser permission the product would ever ask for, so the ask must be user-initiated and revocable. The notification body must never contain a path, a command or message content.
features.localFirstSuitability: Good — the Notification API is local; nothing is sent to a push service, and there must be no service worker or push subscription.
features.macMiniSuitability: This is where it earns its place. A Mac mini running unattended is precisely the case where a finished run needs to reach a person.
features.testPlan: Unit: no Notification constructor is reachable while the switch is off; a denied permission reverts the switch. E2E/static: assert no push, no service worker registration and no subscription endpoint appears anywhere in src/ — this fits the existing no-runtime-contact test.
features.rationale: A product that has never asked the browser for anything should keep that property by default, and only trade it when the owner explicitly decides the unattended case is worth it.

features.name: Checkpoint and rewind
features.userProblem: createCheckpoint and listCheckpoints exist and CheckpointRecord is a real schema entry, so half of this is built. But the schema comment is explicit: 'A checkpoint is a set of references, not a copy.' A checkpoint records where every record was, not what every file contained.
features.proposedBehaviour: Two mutually exclusive designs, and the owner has to choose. (A) Rewind rewinds Forge's own records only — the conversation, task states and run history return to the checkpoint, and the screen says clearly that the working tree was not touched and git is where you undo files. (B) Rewind also restores files, which means adding a restoreCheckpoint operation, a content store, and giving the bridge write access to the working tree. Shipping (A) with a button labelled 'Rewind' without the sentence would be a half-true status of exactly the kind the state machines exist to prevent.
features.securityImpact: Design (B) is the largest single expansion of authority in this whole matrix: it makes the browser able to overwrite the owner's files from a stored snapshot. Design (A) has almost none.
features.localFirstSuitability: Good for (A). For (B), a content store on local disk grows without bound unless it is content-addressed and pruned.
features.macMiniSuitability: (A) is fine. (B) on a small internal SSD needs a hard retention policy before it is written, not after.
features.testPlan: For (A): unit tests that a rewind changes no path on disk, and a UI test that the 'files were not restored' sentence is present and not dismissible. For (B): the full path-guard vector suite plus a test that restore refuses when any recorded hash no longer matches.
features.rationale: The two designs differ in whether the workspace may write to the owner's source files, which is a decision about what this product is, not about how to build it.

features.name: Per-project permissions
features.userProblem: SettingsView draws a four-level permission model (read-only / standard / elevated / lead) and three guard switches, all inert. The contract has PERMISSION_REQUIRED, PERMISSION_DENIED, approveAction and denyAction. Nothing joins the two, so there is no answer to 'is this project allowed to run the toolchain'.
features.proposedBehaviour: A permission policy recorded per project, evaluated by the bridge before a run starts and before any elevated action. Deny by default; a project is granted a level explicitly and the grant is recorded in the audit ledger with a timestamp. The 'Allow shell commands' switch in particular decides whether an agent may execute the project toolchain at all.
features.securityImpact: This is the authority model. Getting the default wrong — inherit rather than deny, or a UI that can widen a grant without an audit line — undermines every other guarantee in the bridge.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — a local policy file evaluated by a local bridge.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent, and more important there: an unattended box should have a narrower default than one someone is watching.
features.testPlan: Unit: default is deny for every level above read-only; a grant produces an audit line; a run that exceeds its grant fails with PERMISSION_DENIED and does not partially execute. E2E: with shell disallowed, runApprovedTest is refused and the refusal reason is shown.
features.rationale: Only the owner can decide what a project is allowed to do to their machine, and that decision has to precede the implementation rather than follow it.

features.name: Safe folder upload
features.userProblem: Attaching a whole folder feels like the obvious way to give a conversation context.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built. The alternative already exists and is better: listProjectFiles and readProjectFile let Claude Code be pointed at the folder where it lives, without copying anything into the attachment store.
features.securityImpact: High if built. Every file in a folder goes through detection, hashing and the 63 KB policy, and one dropped node_modules or .git is thousands of files hashed and scanned. It also multiplies the chance of a secret being copied into the attachment store, which is precisely what policy.ts exists to prevent one file at a time.
features.localFirstSuitability: Poor — it duplicates the owner's files inside the workspace for no gain, since the originals are already on the same disk.
features.macMiniSuitability: Poor. On a fanless box a folder drop is a self-inflicted denial of service and a duplicate copy of a tree that is already local.
features.rationale: Copying a tree into an attachment store to give context to a tool that can already read the tree in place is cost without capability.

features.name: Attachment content search
features.userProblem: Finding which attachment contained a particular string.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built. Attachment filenames fall out of universal-search for free; contents do not get indexed.
features.securityImpact: Indexing attachment contents means reading and retaining text from arbitrary user files — including the ones the pipeline marked QUARANTINE. A search index is a second copy of exactly the data policy.ts spent 63 KB deciding not to trust.
features.localFirstSuitability: Poor — the index would be the largest thing in the workspace and the least verifiable.
features.macMiniSuitability: Poor — sustained disk and CPU on a low-power box for a rare query.
features.rationale: The one part with real value — finding an attachment by name — is already covered, and the rest builds an unauditable second copy of untrusted content.

features.name: Duplicate detection
features.userProblem: Two conversations or two projects that cover the same ground clutter the lists.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: There is no definition of 'duplicate' over this data that survives contact with it — two threads with similar titles are usually two different attempts — and a workspace that claims things are duplicates and is wrong spends the credibility that its evidence-backed claims are earning elsewhere.

features.name: Project scratchpad
features.userProblem: Somewhere to keep loose notes about a project.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built.
features.securityImpact: Low.
features.localFirstSuitability: Neutral — it would be a local text file either way.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: A pane of unversioned, unverified free text sitting beside a proof ledger dilutes the one thing that makes this workspace different, and the project already has .claude/FORGE_MEMORY.md and FORGE_DECISIONS.md for exactly this.

features.name: Prompt library
features.userProblem: Retyping the same instructions into the composer.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built as a library. The real artefacts already exist on disk — .claude/commands/*.md and .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md — and what is missing is reaching them from the composer, which is tracked separately as composer-command-completion.
features.securityImpact: Low.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: It would add a fourteenth destination and a second store for text the workspace already has on disk in a better format.

features.name: Composer command and skill completion
features.userProblem: DISCOVERED, and the honest replacement for prompt-library. The composer has three menus (attach, context, skills) whose contents are hard-coded arrays of four example strings each, while the workspace folder holds 30 SKILL.md files under .claude/skills/ and 2 slash commands under .claude/commands/ that the composer knows nothing about.
features.proposedBehaviour: Typing '/' at the start of the composer lists the real commands from .claude/commands/; typing '@' lists the real skills. Selecting one inserts its invocation as plain text — the composer never executes anything and never loads a playbook itself. The Skills menu shows what is actually installed instead of four labels.
features.securityImpact: Read-only over a known directory. The listing must never render file contents into the composer — only names and one-line descriptions — so a malicious SKILL.md cannot inject text into a prompt the owner did not write.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — it reads a local directory the workspace already sits inside.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent; the listing is small and cacheable per session.
features.testPlan: Unit: only names and descriptions cross the boundary; a skill with a very long description is truncated rather than inserted whole. E2E: type '/', pick a command, assert its text is in the composer and that nothing was sent.
features.rationale: Worth doing, but it should follow sendMessage being wired for real — completing a composer that cannot yet send is decoration.

features.name: Conversation branches
features.userProblem: Wanting to try a second approach from the middle of a thread without losing the first.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. ConversationRecord.claudeSessionId is a single nullable string and the installed CLI's resume is linear, so a branch today means starting a fresh session seeded with a replayed transcript — which loses the prompt cache, spends the owner's quota twice, and produces a second session that only looks like a continuation.
features.securityImpact: Low.
features.localFirstSuitability: Good in principle — branches are local records.
features.macMiniSuitability: Poor while it requires a full transcript replay per branch; that is real tokens and real time on every fork.
features.rationale: Reopen when ClaudeCodeStatus.supportedFlags shows the installed CLI can fork or seed a session while keeping its cache; until then the honest version costs a full re-read of the conversation every time.

features.name: Context manager
features.userProblem: The composer's '@' menu lists four inert context options and there is no way to see or control what is actually in the model's context window.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. UsageSnapshot exposes contextTokensUsed, contextWindow and contextPercent, but nothing in the contract reports what is occupying that window item by item, so a 'manager' would be a set of controls over an inventory the workspace cannot see.
dependencies: a per-item context breakdown from the CLI
features.securityImpact: Low.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good.
features.rationale: Reopen when claude.usage carries a per-item context breakdown; until then the honest version is the context meter in the usage bar, which is already scheduled.

features.name: Project health
features.userProblem: getProjectHealth, ProjectHealthState and ProjectRecord.lastDoctorResult exist, and ProjectsView and ProjectOverviewView already render a health meter — from example data.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. Wire the meter to the real getProjectHealth once projects are real, showing the five states plus lastDoctorResult verbatim, and never a composite score derived from values the bridge could not read.
features.securityImpact: Low, provided UNKNOWN and MISSING are rendered as themselves rather than folded into a number.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good if health is computed on open rather than on a timer.
features.rationale: Reopen the moment createProject and importProject are wired — a health score over zero real projects measures nothing.

features.name: Project archive
features.userProblem: Old projects will eventually crowd the sidebar and the projects screen.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. archiveProject, ProjectRecord.archived and the project.archived event all exist; the UI work is a filter and a confirm.
features.securityImpact: Low — archive is a flag, not a delete. It must stay that way; nothing in this product should delete a project.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent.
features.rationale: Reopen when the registry holds more projects than fit in the sidebar without scrolling; archiving an empty registry solves nothing.

features.name: Conversation archive
features.userProblem: Long-running projects accumulate threads and the sidebar shows only the five most recent.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. archiveConversation, ConversationRecord.archived and conversation.archived exist; the UI work is a filter and a confirm.
features.securityImpact: Low.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent.
features.rationale: Reopen at roughly forty conversations in one project; before that, universal search finds an old thread faster than an archive filter does.

features.name: Backup and restore
features.userProblem: The workspace store will eventually hold conversation history, run records and proof that exist nowhere else.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. .forge-workspace/meta/workspace.json and migrations.json exist and src/bridge/storage/atomic.ts already does atomic writes, so the foundation is there; the missing piece is a bounded, versioned export of the whole store and a restore that refuses a schema it does not understand.
features.securityImpact: A full backup contains everything, including absolute paths and any attachment metadata. It must never be produced by default and never written anywhere but a folder the owner picked in that moment.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent, and arguably obligatory for a local-first product with no server copy.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good with a size cap; a single internal SSD is a single point of failure, which is the argument for building this before the store gets large.
features.rationale: Reopen as soon as the store holds anything the owner could not reconstruct — realistically the first real run — and build the export half before the restore half.

features.name: Export a conversation or a report
features.userProblem: Wanting to hand a thread or a run summary to someone who is not sitting at this machine.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred, and deliberately split from export-evidence-bundle. A conversation export is prose containing whatever the owner typed and whatever the model wrote, which is a different redaction problem from a manifest of hashes.
features.securityImpact: Higher than the evidence bundle, because message bodies can contain anything the owner pasted — including credentials. It needs the secret-pattern scan from policy.ts applied to the output, and a preview before the file is written.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent.
features.rationale: Reopen once the evidence bundle has proven the redaction path; exporting free-form prose is the harder half and should not go first.

features.name: Markdown and code preview
features.userProblem: FilesView can show a file's path, size, timestamp and diff, but never the file. readProjectFile exists in the contract and no view calls it. There is also a third markdown renderer situation: src/views/chat/markdown.tsx (14 KB) and a second small one inside ArtifactsView.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. When it happens, the preview pane gains a Contents tab beside the diff, sharing one markdown renderer with the chat view instead of adding a third.
features.securityImpact: Streaming arbitrary file contents into the browser is the largest new read surface in this matrix. It needs a byte cap, a binary refusal, and the same trusted-root check as every other path operation.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good with a hard byte cap; without one, opening a large log will stall the tab.
features.rationale: Reopen after getFileDiff is proven end to end — the diff answers the question you actually have during a run, and it exercises the same path guard at a fraction of the read volume.

features.name: Large-file warnings
features.userProblem: Attaching or previewing something large should say so before you wait for it.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred, because the flow it warns about does not exist yet: the composer's paperclip is three hard-coded example menus and nothing is ever staged. The limits themselves are already enforced server-side — QUOTA_EXCEEDED and ATTACHMENT_REJECTED are in the error union and src/bridge/attachments/policy.ts is 63 KB.
features.securityImpact: Positive — a warning before the hash means less untrusted data enters the pipeline at all.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent, and the warning matters more on a low-power box than on a workstation.
features.rationale: Reopen when attachments are wired at all; you cannot warn about a file in a flow that does not exist.

features.name: Recent attachment library
features.userProblem: Re-attaching the same screenshot or log to a second conversation means finding it on disk again.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. AttachmentRecord.conversationId is required, so attachments are per-conversation by schema and a cross-conversation library is a storage-schema change, not a UI change.
features.securityImpact: Reusing a staged file across conversations widens the blast radius of a single bad file from one thread to several, and the security verdict would have to be re-evaluated per use rather than cached.
features.macMiniSuitability: Good with a retention policy; without one the attachment store only grows.
features.rationale: Reopen when the same file is observed being staged into a second conversation; until attachments work at all, this is a library with nothing in it.

features.name: Offline and degraded mode
features.userProblem: The bridge can be down, degraded, or mid-reconcile, and every view would keep rendering as though its data were current.
features.proposedBehaviour: Partly in flight — a shell-level connection banner is being built in a parallel work package. What remains is the per-surface half: each view stating when its data is a last-known snapshot rather than a live read, and disabling only the controls that genuinely require the bridge instead of greying out whole screens.
dependencies: the shell connection banner (parallel work package)
features.securityImpact: None directly. The risk is presentational and serious: stale data rendered as live is the same class of error as an unevidenced status.
features.localFirstSuitability: Excellent — 'offline' here means the local bridge, not the internet, which is the only sense that matters for this product.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent, and the case it exists for: a bridge that dies at 3am on an unattended box.
features.testPlan: Deferred with the feature; the existing tests/e2e/no-network.spec.ts is the right place for it.
features.rationale: The shell banner already covers most of the value; per-view treatment should follow the failures actually observed once the bridge is live, rather than being designed against imagined ones.

features.name: Accessibility profiles
features.userProblem: Bundling accessibility choices into named profiles so they can be applied together.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. The shell already does a great deal without a profile abstraction: a skip link, focus trapping in the drawer and palette, roving focus in menus and the file tree, aria-activedescendant on the palette combobox, a polite log limited to additions in MessageList, visually-hidden descriptions on every change marker, status that never depends on colour, and prefers-reduced-motion honoured alongside an explicit switch.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: Reopen against a real need the current tokens cannot meet; a profiles abstraction built speculatively is a settings construct with no user behind it.

features.name: Per-project model defaults
features.userProblem: Wanting a project to default to a particular model or effort level.
features.proposedBehaviour: Deferred. The workspace does not route models — USES_ANTHROPIC_API is false and the CLI chooses. UsageSnapshot.model is EXACT because the CLI reported it, not because the workspace requested it. A default the workspace cannot enforce would be a setting that lies.
features.securityImpact: Low.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: Reopen when ClaudeCodeStatus.supportedFlags reports a model flag the installed CLI accepts — the adapter is already gated on that list, so the precondition is mechanically checkable rather than a matter of opinion.

features.name: Event gap detection surface
features.userProblem: DISCOVERED. ForgeEvent.sequence is monotonic per stream and the protocol comment says this is 'what makes gap detection possible — the client can prove it missed something instead of silently rendering an incomplete story'. No view shows a gap. The mechanism is designed and unused.
features.proposedBehaviour: The Activity timeline and the Dock event stream render a visible break where a sequence gap occurred, stating how many events are missing and offering replayEvents to fill it. ConversationRecord.lastConfirmedSequence is the anchor.
features.securityImpact: None. It is purely an honesty mechanism.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent — an unattended box is exactly where a gap happens and nobody notices.
features.testPlan: Deferred with the feature; drop a sequence in a fixture and assert the break renders and replay closes it.
features.rationale: Reopen alongside the degraded-mode work — a gap indicator and a connection state are the same story told at two scales, and building them separately would produce two vocabularies for one problem.

features.name: Static icon map
features.userProblem: DISCOVERED (debt, not a feature). Icon.tsx resolves lucide icons by runtime name, which defeats tree-shaking and puts the whole icon set in the bundle: 1.23 MB JS, 343 KB gzipped.
features.proposedBehaviour: Replace name-based resolution with an explicit map of the icons actually used, generated and checked the same way brand/build-theme.cjs checks the CSS — a build step that fails when a view references an icon the map does not contain.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.localFirstSuitability: Neutral — the bundle is served from the same disk it lives on.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral today. It becomes real the moment the workspace is packaged or served to anything but localhost.
features.testPlan: Deferred with the feature; the check step is the test.
features.rationale: Reopen before packaging or any non-localhost delivery; on a local machine reading its own disk, 343 KB gzipped costs nothing measurable and the change touches every view.

features.name: Diff review with per-hunk approval
features.userProblem: Wanting to accept some of a change and not the rest.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built. Diff review already exists — FilesView parses and renders a unified diff with a numbered gutter and add/remove labelling, and getFileDiff is in the contract. Per-hunk approval is the other half, and it means writing to the working tree.
features.securityImpact: It turns the bridge from an observer of the working tree into a mutator of it, which is a whole new class of path and concurrency risk — an applied hunk against a file that changed underneath produces a corrupted source file with no record of what happened.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: Git already does per-hunk staging correctly and the workspace already reads GitState, so this would be a second, weaker version of a tool the owner has open in the next window — and it would buy that duplication with the largest authority expansion on the board.

features.name: Focus mode
features.userProblem: Wanting a quieter screen.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: The shell already collapses the sidebar (Ctrl+B), the inspector and the dock independently; a focus mode is a fourth control whose only job is to press the other three, which is more interface for no new capability.

features.name: Multi-panel workspace
features.userProblem: Wanting two views side by side.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Poor — more simultaneously mounted views on a low-power box.
features.rationale: The shell is already four regions on one CSS grid with two responsive breakpoints; user-splittable panes mean every one of the 13 views must work at arbitrary widths, which multiplies the responsive test matrix that tests/e2e/responsive.spec.ts currently covers at seven fixed sizes.

features.name: Customizable layout
features.userProblem: Wanting to rearrange the shell.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built beyond what exists: the sidebar, inspector and dock are each independently toggleable, the dock has six selectable panels, and the two densest views (Agents, Tasks) already offer three and four layouts respectively.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: Same family as multi-panel: the arrangement is a considered design with a documented breakpoint behaviour, and making it user-defined trades that for a configuration surface nobody asked for.

features.name: Reduced-detail mode
features.userProblem: Wanting less information on screen.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: Density already provides one 'less' axis and it is wired end to end; a second, semantically different 'less' means every view has to decide what counts as detail, and two views will decide differently.

features.name: Advanced operator mode
features.userProblem: Hiding complexity from a beginner and revealing it to an expert.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built.
features.securityImpact: A mode that hides evidence is a mode in which a user can be shown a status without the material that justifies it.
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: This product's central rule is that a screen may only render what the bridge could prove; a mode whose purpose is to render less of the proof is in direct conflict with it, and it doubles the surface every future feature has to be designed against.

features.name: Theme density
features.userProblem: Fitting more rows on a laptop screen.
features.proposedBehaviour: Already shipped. A SegmentedControl in Settings → Appearance and in the topbar account popover writes data-density on the document root, retunes control heights, row heights and gutters through the tokens, and persists to forge.prototype.density.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent.
features.testPlan: Already covered by the existing suites.
features.rationale: There is nothing to build — it is done, wired and persisted, and reopening it would only add options nobody has asked for.

features.name: Recent and pinned items
features.userProblem: Getting back to what you were working on.
features.proposedBehaviour: Already shipped in three places: pinned and recent projects plus recent conversations in the sidebar, recent-file chips in FilesView, and 'Continue working' on Home. The genuine gap is that pins live in memory and die on reload, which is covered by workspace-preference-persistence.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Excellent.
features.rationale: The feature exists; only its persistence is missing, and that is a separate, smaller item that should not be re-litigated as a new feature.

features.name: Agent timeline
features.userProblem: Seeing which agent was doing what, when.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built as a separate surface. ActivityView already groups 47 event types by run with a per-agent filter, an agent column and a sticky run header; MissionControlView already draws the same run as a lane graph with verification and the repair loop routed underneath.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.macMiniSuitability: Poor — a continuously re-laid-out Gantt is the most expensive way to render the same events.
features.rationale: It would be a third rendering of one event stream, and three representations of the same truth is how they start disagreeing.

features.name: Task dependency graph
features.userProblem: Understanding why a task is blocked.
features.proposedBehaviour: Not built as a fifth layout. Task.dependencies already exists on every task in the data and MissionControl already draws edges of kind 'dependency'. The cheap correct answer is to render the dependency list inline on the task card and in the inspector, with each entry linking to its task and showing its status — a change measured in dozens of lines, inside a layout that already exists.
features.securityImpact: None.
features.complexity: L as a graph, S as an inline list
features.macMiniSuitability: Neutral.
features.rationale: TasksView already carries four layouts and Mission Control already is the graph; a fifth layout that draws the same edges in a second place is duplication, whereas the inline dependency list answers the actual question for a fraction of the work.
